title: ‘Abbott Elementary’ Star William Stanford Davis Sets Memoir ‘Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: William Stanford Davis, who stars in “Abbott Elementary” as the janitor Mr. Johnson, is publishing a memoir titled “Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid” vi
body:
William Stanford Davis, who stars in “Abbott Elementary” as the janitor Mr. Johnson, is publishing a memoir titled “Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid” via BenBella Books.

	“Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid” will dive into Davis’ life and career — including struggles such as addiction and rejection — and the experience of nabbing his breakout role at age 70. Per the official description, Davis’ story is written in three parts: “The first will chronicle Davis’ childhood in the 1960s in the Ville, a predominantly Black neighborhood in St. Louis. The second will follow him as a young man, fresh off the bus in ‘country-ass’ Jefferson City in the early 1970s. The final section will chronicle Davis’ journey, well into his forties, from addict to working actor, and the years of perseverance, rejection and hard-earned experience that ultimately led to the biggest role of his career.”
	

	“Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid” was sold to BenBella Books editor and CEO Glen Yeffeth by Miles Blim at Aevitas Creative Management in association with Innovative Artists. It will be released in hardcover, e-book, and audiobook formats.


	Besides “Abbott Elementary,” Davis’ credits include the Wanda Sykes film “Undercard,” Apple TV’s “Swagger,” HBO’s “Curb Your Enthusiasm,” Showtime’s “Ray Donovan” and ABC’s “Lincoln Heights.” 

	“I’ve wanted to write this memoir for a long time, to honor the road I’ve taken to get here and to connect with folks who are still on their way,” Davis said in a statement. “People know me as Mr. Johnson from ‘Abbott Elementary,’ and while that’s the biggest role of my career so far, it’s not the whole story. I’m excited to finally share the full story: the struggles, the setbacks, the second chances and the perseverance it took to keep going and get to where I am today. It took me a long time to get here, and the beautiful thing is, I’m just getting started.”

schema.headline: ‘Abbott Elementary’ Star William Stanford Davis Sets Memoir ‘Don’t Mess With the Fat Kid’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Lanterns’ Season 2 Won’t Be Greenlit Until the Writers’ Room ‘Comes Up With a Worthy Successor to a Great First Season’
description: While HBO’s “Lanterns” hasn’t yet scored a second season renewal, one could be on the way depending on how things go in the writers’ room, accordin
body:
While HBO’s “Lanterns” hasn’t yet scored a second season renewal, one could be on the way depending on how things go in the writers’ room, according to DC Studios co-chief Peter Safran. 

	While he didn’t confirm an exact date fans can expect an announcement to come on, Safran did note that news on whether “Lanterns” will get a second season should arrive “before the end of the year” in a recent interview with Collider. Safran also noted that Season 2 would need to be up to par with Season 1, which enjoyed a massively successful premiere and run. “If we’re able to come up with what we believe to be a worthy successor to a beloved and great first season, that’s what’s going to dictate whether there’s a second season,” he said.
	

	Safran added that the most rewarding part of Season 1’s success has been seeing the “Green Lantern” property back in the cultural conversation. (“Lanterns” was adapted from DC Comics’ “Green Lantern” franchise, which follows an intergalactic police force.)


	The eight-episode show’s season finale aired on Oct. 4, and wrapped up the central mystery of who killed Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) and revealed the identity of the second Manhunter, plus how John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) becomes Earth’s sole Green Lantern in DC Studios’ forthcoming “Superman” sequel, “Man of Tomorrow.”

	Before the finale, Variety reported that the show’s seventh episode reached 7 million viewers in the U.S. in its first three days of availability. Previous episodes had averaged over 12 million viewers per episode in the U.S. to date and nearly 19 million when factoring in international viewing.

schema.headline: ‘Lanterns’ Season 2 Won’t Be Greenlit Until the Writers’ Room ‘Comes Up With a Worthy Successor to a Great First Season’

title: ’60 Minutes’ Sees Audience Dip Without NFL Lead-In
description:
What was all the fuss about?

	An average of 6.06 million people tuned in to watch an episode of “60 Minutes” that became the spark of an intense d
body:
What was all the fuss about?

	An average of 6.06 million people tuned in to watch an episode of “60 Minutes” that became the spark of an intense debate between longtime correspondent Lesley Stahl and CBS News Editor in Chief Bari Weiss, who wrangled with one another over the content of Stahl’s segment centered on Israeli settlers seeking to drive out Palestinians on the West Bank, according to a person familiar with the matter. The dispute over the report, which tackled an issue close to Weiss, forced CBS News to delay promotion of the episode and angered Stahl, who felt compelled to defend her reporting at a late stage of production. The Status media newsletter previously reported details of the struggle between Weiss and Stahl.
	

	The 6.06 million figure represents a 12% decline in viewership from the last season’s fourth episode of the show, according to Nielsen, and a nearly 41% dip from last week’s audience, which was boosted by a record-setting NFL game that aired before the Sunday newsmagazine. The new episode of “60 Minutes” also faced competition from an NFL game airing on Fox and NBC’s NFL pre-game show, which began in the middle of the episode.


	The telecast also saw declines among people between the ages of 25 and 54, the demographic most coveted by advertisers in news programming. Sunday’s episode wooed an average of 767,000, compared with 946,000 a year earlier, and 2.02 million last week. The demo ratings declined nearly 19% from last season and 62% from last week’s telecast, according to data from Nielsen.

	CBS News remains under intense pressure to demonstrate stability at the program, which was overhauled in chaotic fashion at the end of last season, despite mustering a notable 9% uptick in overall viewership. Weiss ousted Tanya Simon, an executive producer with years of history working at the show, in favor of Nick Bilton, a journalist and screenwriter with less formal TV experience. Also pushed out were correspondents Scott Pelley, Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi. Anderson Cooper left of his own volition following the end of his contract. Their replacements, which include Ross Douthat and contributors like Ariel Levy and Sebastian Junger, have top-shelf backgrounds, but also little experience working on a weekly TV program that emphasizes long-form enterprise journalism.
	

	CBS can take some solace from the fact that Sunday’s “60 Minutes” telecast gained viewers throughout the episode, according to Nielsen data. 

	In addition to Stahl’s report from the West Bank, Sunday’s episode also featured a report an interview by Norah O’Donnell of Sean Curran and Matt Quinn, director and deputy director of the U.S. Secret Service, The show’s third segment focused on Bill Whitaker’s profile of musician Jon Batiste.

schema.headline: ’60 Minutes’ Sees Audience Dip Without NFL Lead-In

title: Critics Vindicate ‘Artificial’ After Messy Amazon MGM Breakup (and the Studios vs. Talent Wars Around AI Are Just Beginning)
description:
Looks like “Artificial” is the real thing.

	Luca Guadagnino’s genre-blending movie about the evils of artificial intelligence (and one of its fath
body:
Looks like “Artificial” is the real thing.

	Luca Guadagnino’s genre-blending movie about the evils of artificial intelligence (and one of its fathers, Sam Altman) had a triumphant U.K. premiere at the London Film Festival on Sunday. The director, standing beside key cast members Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov, received thunderous applause at Royal Festival Hall.

	The British event followed the world premiere of “Artificial” a week earlier at the New York Film Festival. It was a make-or-break moment for a project plagued by scandal after Amazon MGM punted the film off its summer slate. Worse was what came after: an odious whisper campaign saying the film stank (anonymous sources dismissed it as only worthy of a streaming release, according to a July report). But the Big Apple swallowed the film with rapture.
	

	“So this is a dawn-of-a-new-world story, as well as a backstabbing corporate business story, and also a horror movie, in which AI emerges from the lab as a sinister serpent,” wrote Variety chief critic Owen Gleiberman in his review, calling the movie a “brilliant but playful docudrama, meticulously true to history.”


	Others agree. The title has a 96% Fresh rating on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes, representing the highest score of Guadagnino’s career across 11 feature film releases. Garfield has been catapulted to the front of the best supporting actor race, thanks to a performance that delivers “a masterclass in diabolical villainy,” according to another review.

	The notices, the standing ovations, the awards buzz — all of it represents a stunning reversal of fortune for Guadagnino after the Amazon debacle in June. It was highly uncommon, in Hollywood terms, for even a tech-owned content studio to kill a project it had cradled since infancy. Neon rescued the movie with a global rights deal shortly after the Amazon rift.
	

	“We believe that ‘Artificial’ will be better served if it were released by a different studio,” the e-commerce giant said at the time. Global press almost unanimously noted that the decision to jettison the movie came only three months after Amazon signed a significant partnership with Altman’s OpenAI (including a $50 billion investment in the company).

	But, per Variety’s sources, the writing is on the wall. Nothing was wrong with “Artificial,” and the response underlines the dubiousness of Amazon’s decision to drop it. 

	“Wasn’t this supposed to be god-awful?” wondered one film executive at a rival studio. The exec didn’t just raise an eyebrow at Amazon MGM, but at other legacy distributors who were in the mix to take the project before Neon won out. “A reaction this strong just shows you, every studio pretending the film wasn’t releasable is just conflicted out by their own investments in AI.”

	In July, New York magazine published a piece citing individuals close to the project as saying it “lacked theater-worthy criteria.” That doesn’t quite track with early audience response. In fact, the critical consensus is that “Artificial” — not Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” which debuted last weekend via Sony Pictures — is a worthy spiritual successor to David Fincher’s “The Social Network.” It’s hard to imagine Amazon not being pleased with this response had it kept “Artificial.”

	Interestingly, Amazon’s headaches at the intersection of talent and AI are not exclusive to the Guadagnino movie. At New York Comic Con last weekend, actor Nicolas Cage made waves when he disclosed that he refused to sign a document permitting the studio to use AI in and around his likeness on its now-canceled original series “Spider-Noir.”

	“I am not an AI-friendly actor. I’m not a member of their club. I didn’t sign the waiver,” Cage said. “I’m probably not going to be working with that studio again.” There’s a bit more to this story, insiders close to “Spider-Noir” said. Cage was referring to a form from the show’s producer, Sony Pictures Television, considered “industry standard” on content shoots. The waiver gives the studio permission to create a duplicate of an actor in costume, which aids in VFX work during postproduction. Actors are free to opt out, and the form is said to be in line with SAG-AFTRA guidelines.
	

	But it won’t be the end of talent bristling over the coming AI revolution — at Amazon or elsewhere. One creative team member on an Amazon MGM series tells Variety that AI training is a requirement on the lot these days.

	The source describes a “mandatory and perfunctory meeting” with the company’s AI team, billed as standard workplace education that corporations regularly hold around sexual harassment and fire safety. The AI group spent an hour pitching the creatives on a suite of products it referred to as “tools.” Our source says, however, it became clear that these tools could “eliminate entire jobs” on the production. Amazon MGM declined to comment on the matter.

	More telling, per the source, is that the show’s corporate stewards from Amazon also sat through the training “stone-faced.” While the individual won’t name the execs in attendance, they found it “collectively embarrassing for everyone to be doing this, including on the Amazon side.” A source with direct knowledge of Amazon’s process said such meetings are not mandatory, and humans guide every part of the process related to the tools. 

	And so begins the great sacrifice the major studios are about to make in service of computer-based cost efficiencies and the “move fast and break things” bravado of Silicon Valley. Time will tell if a prompt can make content that’s as buzzy and well positioned as “Artificial.”

schema.headline: Critics Vindicate ‘Artificial’ After Messy Amazon MGM Breakup (and the Studios vs. Talent Wars Around AI Are Just Beginning)

title: ‘Beach Fictions’ Review: Utterly Beguiling, Time-Tweaking Korean Romance Shows What a Day a Difference Makes
description: Fatalism, self-determination and imagination all gently wrestle for control of the narrative(s) in “Beach Fictions,” an enchanting and subtly profo
body:
Fatalism, self-determination and imagination all gently wrestle for control of the narrative(s) in “Beach Fictions,” an enchanting and subtly profound diptych that follows one young woman through two diverging versions of the same day — saying much in the process about the voices, inner and otherwise, that we grant most control in our lives, for better or worse. Though its structuring principle of a single day playing out twice consecutively to differing effect (as opposed to braiding its alternate timelines like “Sliding Doors” or “Blind Chance”) explicitly recalls Hong Sangsoo’s “Right Now, Wrong Then,” this chicly poised debut feature by fellow South Korean Lim Hayeon has a style, tone and outlook of its own, maintained with impressive control over a surprisingly breezy-feeling 145 minutes.
	

	One of the real discoveries in this year’s main competition at the Busan Film Festival, “Beach Fictions” should have little difficulty charming other programmers on the international fest circuit following its world premiere — while only its running time, manageable but unexpectedly robust for a film this light on its feet, presents an obstacle to global arthouse distribution, or at least specialist streaming exposure. Either way, this graduation project (produced by the  Korean Academy of Film Arts) announces its writer-director-editor as one to watch, should her future films match this one’s warmth and formal elegance; in only her second big-screen outing after years of TV work, winsome lead Hansol Park also feels like a breakout talent.


	“Beach Fictions” pulls you in from its first iridescent frame, as Sinuk Park’s camera glides serenely from a bejeweled nighttime view of Incheon through the chattery hubbub of a mood-lit restaurant where Tae-ju (Park), seen only from behind, is dining with friends, their conversation seemingly more animated than hers. Even without the detached voiceover — which turns out to belong to perceptive novelist Ewha (Sujeong Ye), describing the superficial response of Tae-ju’s friends to an anecdote she shares — we’d sense her loneliness amid company. Later, when her friends abandon her at the table to smoke outside, she’s crushed to find them gossiping about her; shortly afterwards, in a never-rains-but-pours development, she breaks up with her casual boyfriend Hyun-jin after he expresses scant interest in taking the relationship further.
	

	With her social life in tatters and a world of her anxieties realized, Tae-ju rashly skips town, heading for the tranquil coastal guesthouse of another friend. On the train there, she encounters Ewha, whom we’ve already seen observing her from afar at the restaurant, and confides in the kindly, silver-haired older woman — who says Tae-ju resembles the protagonist of the novel she’s currently writing. But is she the  writer’s inspiration or her creation, an incomplete fiction who has somehow taken on an agency of her own? From here on out, the authorship of Tae-ju’s life is ambiguous, as well as constantly in flux, buffeted by the whims and suggestions of others, as well as by her own impulses.

	In the sleepy beach town, she meets and is immediately entranced by charismatic street magician Manhyuk (Kim Wookyum, delightful), only to later be warned off him by her hostess, who claims he’s a local lothario and sometime sex worker. A day in his company turns sour but when, in the film’s deftly shuffled second half, she meets him in slightly different circumstances, and the day’s events take on a different chain of connections, the potential romantic outcome differs too. 

	Her nascent relationship with Manhyuk is the chief variable of Tae-ju’s two stories, but other, slighter factors push it this way and that: a water-damaged phone in need of repair; a hangout with fellow guesthouse patrons that echoes or corrects her earlier social fallout; and a consultation with a psychic, recommended by Ehwa, whose counsel also shifts her fate. The contrasts between the two tales are never drastic; the gradations are sometimes as fine as those between warm and cool melancholy. The camerawork is consistently, richly sun-flooded, but some compositions isolate Tae-ju more than others; Wonhong Lee’s delicate jazz piano score can similarly tilt a situation from cozy to nervy.

	But both gently lolloping narratives hold the attention, in large part thanks to Park’s deeply sympathetic performance as Hae-ju, simultaneously played as a fragile, will-o’-the-wisp go-alonger — or perhaps just an author’s as-yet-unformed blank canvas — and a wounded flesh-and-blood human now guarding her emotions more carefully. It’s a canny turn completely in synch with Lim’s complex, metatextual script, which brims with ideas about the fictional construction process, as well the real-life bind felt by vulnerable young women expected to bend to others’ desires and expectations. Is life itself not just a series of drafts and redrafts, with notes we either learn from or don’t, our characters never not in progress? Wry and wise and happy-sad, “Beach Fictions” crosses nothing out, alive to all possibilities.

schema.headline: ‘Beach Fictions’ Review: Utterly Beguiling, Time-Tweaking Korean Romance Shows What a Day a Difference Makes

title: Fox’s $22 Billion Roku Deal Approved by Shareholders of Both Companies
description: In an expected development, shareholders for both Fox Corp. and Roku voted to approve Fox’s $22 billion acquisition of the streaming-video platform
body:
In an expected development, shareholders for both Fox Corp. and Roku voted to approve Fox’s $22 billion acquisition of the streaming-video platform company.

	At separate special meetings of shareholders Wednesday to vote on the deal, the majority of shares owned by Fox Corp. and Roku investors were in favor the deal. 

	The proposed Roku deal was overwhelmingly approved by Fox shareholders: 99.9% of the votes cast by holders of outstanding Class B common stock entitled to vote were in favor of the agreement, according to an SEC filing by Fox. Of the shares voted, 197.4 million were for; 71,891 were against; and 45,001 abstained. The official vote tallies from Roku’s meeting are expected to be filed with the SEC soon as well.
	

	In June, Fox announced an agreement to buy Roku for $160/share in a combination of about $14.2 billion in cash and the remainder in Fox Class A common stock.


	Fox currently expects the Roku acquisition to be completed in the first half of calendar year 2027, subject to clearance by the Justice Department and other regulators. 

	Last month, Fox disclosed that the DOJ had requested additional documents related to the proposed Roku acquisition, which Fox said was expected. The DOJ’s second request for documents extended the waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino antitrust act for 30 days (during which time the parties are barred from closing the deal) after Fox and Roku have “substantially replied” to the information request.

	The deal would dramatically enhance Fox’s streaming footprint, and give it the opportunity to increase scale in the free, ad-supported streaming space through Fox’s Tubi and the Roku Channel. By buying Roku, the TV-centric company would become a much bigger player in digital video advertising as well as major player in premium subscription VOD distribution.
	

	The Roku acquisition “will transform the scope of our company into high-growth verticals and yield a step change in our overall growth profile,” Fox Corp. CEO Lachlan Murdoch said in announcing the agreement in June.

	Fox said it is “committed to continuing to operate Roku as an open, partner-friendly platform.” Roku founder and CEO Anthony Wood will have an ongoing role at the combined company.

schema.headline: Fox’s $22 Billion Roku Deal Approved by Shareholders of Both Companies

title: Sally Rooney Speaks Out on Her Books Being Removed from U.K. Shelves Over Palestine Action Support: ‘I Am Wholly Prepared to Accept the Consequences’
description:
Sally Rooney is sticking to her guns.

	The Irish author behind the bestselling novels “Conversations with Friends” and “Normal People” — the latte
body:
Sally Rooney is sticking to her guns.

	The Irish author behind the bestselling novels “Conversations with Friends” and “Normal People” — the latter adapted into an award-winning miniseries that launched the careers of Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones — has claimed spoken out about being forced to not sell her books in the U.K. over her support for Palestine Action, a banned direct action network that has been labeled a “terrorist group” in the U.K. under Terrorism Act 2000.
	

	Palestine Action uses direct action protests with the goal of “ending global participation in Israel’s genocidal and apartheid regime.” When Palestine Action was banned and labeled a “terrorist group” last year, the 35-year-old author stated that she would be using proceeds from her book sales to support the organization. She also canceled a trip to England last year to pick up an award (and all future public appearances there) for fear of being arrested. 


	“In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organization in the U.K. The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland,” Rooney said in a statement.

	She continued: “As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the U.K. could now constitute a serious criminal offence. After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the U.K. I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”
	

	Rooney’s publisher in the U.K. and Ireland, Faber, echoed Rooney’s claims in a similar statement:

	“Current legislation in the U.K. has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on U.K. earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher. As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the U.K. in any format. We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories.”

	Since Hamas massacred over 1,200 people on Oct. 7, 2023, retaliatory attacks by the Israeli military on Gaza have reportedly claimed the lives of over 75,000 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.

	In her Aug. 2025 op-ed for the Irish Times defending her contributions to Palestine Action, Rooney wrote, “Palestine Action has been among the strongest of those voices in the UK, taking direct steps to halt the seemingly unstoppable machinery of violence. We owe their courageous activists our gratitude and solidarity. And by now, almost two years into a live-streamed genocide, we owe the people of Palestine more than mere words.”

schema.headline: Sally Rooney Speaks Out on Her Books Being Removed from U.K. Shelves Over Palestine Action Support: ‘I Am Wholly Prepared to Accept the Consequences’

title: Markus Schleinzer on Sandra Hüller, Star of His Austrian Oscar Entry ‘Rose’ and a Berlin Best Lead Performance Winner: ‘She’s the Queen’
description:
As a filmmaker, Markus Schleinzer owes much to his 17-year career as a casting director. 

	“Directing a movie and being a casting director are qui
body:
As a filmmaker, Markus Schleinzer owes much to his 17-year career as a casting director. 

	“Directing a movie and being a casting director are quite similar jobs,” he tells Variety.

	Both require making the right choices under pressure and persuading others to believe in them. For a casting director, that means convincing a filmmaker or producer. For a director, it means earning the audience’s trust.


	Schleinzer admits that, despite what people might think, he can be rather shy and timid. Casting offered a way to remain somewhat in the background while still being deeply involved in the filmmaking process. For years, he worked closely for Michael Haneke as his casting director. But Haneke also gave Schleinzer opportunities to direct background performers and learn how a film set operates. “He put a lot of trust in me,” he says.
	

	Haneke was also the one who urged him to step out from behind the scenes and become a filmmaker himself, giving him three months to write a script.

	“I thought, yes, this was a compliment,” Schleinzer recalls. “But three months later he called me and said, ‘Where’s the script?’ And I didn’t have a single line.”

	Eventually, he sat down and wrote one. Haneke liked it and refused to let it languish in a drawer, passing it along to French producer Margaret Ménégoz, who called Schleinzer to say she wanted to make it.“So I was trapped,” he says. “I couldn’t get away from it anymore. This is how I, finally, got kicked in my ass.”

	His third feature, “Rose,” which screened at the Vancouver International Film Festival (VIFF), is a black-and-white historical drama starring Sandra Hüller as a woman who disguises herself as a male soldier in 17th-century Germany. By exposing the contradictions of a society that values people for what they can contribute while restricting who is allowed to contribute, the film turns one woman’s struggle to live freely into a broader indictment of the rules governing gender and belonging.
	

	Schleinzer wrote the role specifically for Hüller, whose performance continues to move him even after countless viewings.

	“She’s the queen,” he says. “I’ve seen it in post-production, whatever, I’ve seen it a hundred times. Still, there were moments, there were sentences, there were scenes, where she completely moves me, where I start to cry, where I get angry again, like an audience member who sees this for the very first time. And that’s the craft she’s owning. That’s her superpower she’s owning.”

	The film began as a sprawling prose work of roughly 1,000 pages, tracing Rose’s life from early childhood. Of course, Schleinzer understood that no one was going to spend millions making a 45-hour film. “So, we just skipped the first eight hundred pages and we just concentrated on the last two hundred because the ending of the novel could stand for itself.”

	When Hüller read it, she told him: “You are crazy. This is not a script. That’s a poem.”

	If there is a through line in Schleinzer’s work, it is his fascination with people on the margins.“Where we are as a society, how we deal with our so-called outsiders, what kind of society we are is quite interesting for me,” he says. With “Rose,” he turns his attention to what he considers the largest outsider group in the world: women.

	The idea grew out of a conversation with a friend who called to wish him a happy birthday and mentioned having just finished a book about a woman executed on that same date roughly 250 years earlier. Her alleged transgression? Wearing trousers.

	The story sent Schleinzer researching the archives, where he unearthed numerous accounts of women who disguised themselves as men for a range of reasons. Some wanted to escape unwanted marriages and sexual harassment. Others did so to gain access to education, employment and military service. Some may have also been lesbian or transgender, he suggests.

	In England, Schleinzer notes, one woman rose to a senior officer’s rank and fought for the British Empire. It was only at the officer’s funeral that it was discovered that the person they had bestowed all these medals on was, in fact, a woman.

	More than historical curiosities, such stories reveal how elaborate disguises can become necessary as a means of survival in a world that denies people the freedom to be themselves — both historically and today.
	

	“It’s interesting to see the amount of effort that we put into our daily routine in building up our mask,” he says. “Sometimes how you behave yourself is a mask: how you move, how you want to be read, how you hold your shoulders, how you walk.”

	A mask can function as armor, protecting its wearer. “If it’s something that helps you, I think it’s okay,” he says. “But when it becomes a cage, that’s the weird part of it.”

	He describes “Rose” as a “love letter for all those people who, for various reasons, have to hide who they are, or to serve the community they really want to serve or have to put on a mask to achieve the things they wouldn’t be able to without them. They couldn’t live the fullest life, because we wouldn’t let them.”

	Rose, Schleinzer explains, is not some revolutionary seeking to overthrow the society around her. She simply wants to belong, to work and to serve. The injustice is that she must conceal her identity to do what others are free to do openly.

	“I was born a feminist without knowing,” Schleinzer says. He grew up surrounded by women, and when he started school at seven, he encountered a different set of rules. He remembers realizing that “there is a different system that exists in the world” and it was one he “didn’t like very much.”

	That discomfort informs the film’s treatment of sexual violence, which is present in the story but never shown graphically. Schleinzer made a deliberate choice not to depict the assaults themselves, arguing that images carry a responsibility, particularly in a culture saturated with graphic representations of suffering.

	“The cruelest thing in the world is our own imagination,” he says. “And the more I feed imagination with images like this, the crueler we can get, because we completely lose empathy.”

	For Schleinzer, it is important to acknowledge the violence without turning it into spectacle, trusting viewers to understand its consequences without being shown every physical detail.

	Ultimately, the central question that “Rose” asks isn’t whether people should be allowed to step outside society’s expectations, but rather why it’s so restrictive in the first place — and what might change if people were given the freedom to find their own place.
	

	“The most difficult thing is to find one’s own place,” Schleinzer says, noting that what feels like belonging today may change tomorrow. “We have to accept that change is happening every day. And sometimes we just should give things time to see if this could be a good thing or not.”

	The masks people wear, he suggests, need not be fixed identities or permanent disguises. They can also be a way forward. “So maybe these things we sometimes call masks are just a vehicle for us to get where we have to go.”

schema.headline: Markus Schleinzer on Sandra Hüller, Star of His Austrian Oscar Entry ‘Rose’ and a Berlin Best Lead Performance Winner: ‘She’s the Queen’

title: YouTube to Label AI-Generated Songs Across Its Platforms: Listeners ‘Want Transparency’
description: YouTube will label AI-generated songs across its main website and YouTube Music, the latest service to publicly mark tracks as not produced by huma
body:
YouTube will label AI-generated songs across its main website and YouTube Music, the latest service to publicly mark tracks as not produced by humans.

	“Generative AI is opening up new ways for artists to create, experiment, and share music,” YouTube said in a blog post on Wednesday. “As these tools evolve, our listeners have told us they want transparency when they’re hearing an AI-generated track.”


	The labels began rolling out across YouTube Music on Wednesday, and it will soon expand to the main YouTube platform. The markers will apply to songs YouTube, through its own detection tools and those made by its music partners, deems were “created primarily using generative AI.”
	

	YouTube’s pivot comes as several music streaming services have promised to label tracks made either primarily by AI or through some level of AI assistance. Apple Music said in August it would add “Made by AI” labels to songs later this year, just after Spotify said it would label the profiles of artists who appear to be AI-generated as “AI Personas.” Tidal has also promised to label AI music and ban those tracks from accruing royalties. 

	A collection of groups representing musicians and the music industry at large — including the RIAA, IFPI, the Grammys and SAG-AFTRA — also banded together over the summer to advocate for a new labeling program to indicate whether a song was produced with AI, urging them to use “AI-Generated” or “AI-Assisted” indicators. 

	“Fans want to know whether and how generative AI has been used in the music to which they listen,” International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) CEO Vikki Oakley and Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) chairman and CEO Mitch Glazier said in a statement.

schema.headline: YouTube to Label AI-Generated Songs Across Its Platforms: Listeners ‘Want Transparency’

title: RJ Mitte's Fiancée Wanted Him to Choose Between Her or His Mom Before Death
description:
RJ Mitte
                          Forced to Choose Between Mom and Fiancée ...
body:
RJ Mitte
                          Forced to Choose Between Mom and Fiancée ...
                          Relationship Was On the Rocks
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 14, 2026
                            10:54 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 14, 2026
                                3:42 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            RJ Mitte faced an impossible choice in the days leading up to his death ... multiple sources close to his family tell us his frustrated fiancée gave him an ultimatum -- choose between her and his mom.
      
    
            Our sources tell TMZ ... there was mounting tension between RJ and his fiancée Kennedy Suarez, who felt RJ's mom was meddling in their relationship.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            According to our sources ... Kennedy and RJ's mom, Dyna, did not get along ... and Kennedy wanted RJ to favor her, or else.
      

            RJ had an extremely close relationship with Dyna and his sister, Lacianne... and wasn't willing to cut his mom off ... and that caused serious friction in his relationship with Kennedy.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            RJ and Kennedy were friends for 10 years before they began dating in 2020. They got engaged October 10, 2025, almost a year to the day before he took his life.
      
    
            We're told RJ and Kennedy were still together a week before he died. It's unclear if they broke up in the days before RJ's death.
      
    
            Our sources say in the weeks before RJ's death, his relationship with Kennedy was weighing heavily on him, and he was outwardly distraught.
      
    
            We broke the story ... RJ was found dead in Texas on Monday. A county official told us he died by suicide.
      
    
            A celebration of life for RJ is scheduled for Friday at The Mitte: Arts and Cultural Center in Brownsville, TX.
      
    
            RJ was just 34 years old.
      
    
            If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. Call or text 988 or chat 988lifeline.org.

body:
'7 Little Johnstons' Star Anna
                          Busted for DUI … Cheesing in Mug Shot

                              October 14, 2026
                            3:45 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            "7 Little Johnstons" star Anna Johnston was hauled into jail after being arrested for DUI ... and flashed a big smile for her mug shot.
      
    
            According to a police report obtained by multiple outlets, Anna was arrested in Georgia on Saturday after cops saw her car parked on the side of the highway and investigated. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The report says Anna was driving her boyfriend, Jeffrey Messervy, and his cousin when she got into an argument with Jeffrey and pulled over. They say Jeffrey told them he was "upset due to Anna driving them around with alcohol in her system."
      
    
            Anna was allegedly slurring her speech when the officer arrived and was asked to take a breathalyzer ... and cops say she blew a 0.139. Police say she reeked of booze and bombed a field sobriety test, so they arrested her for DUI. 
      

                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The day after her DUI bust, Anna was released from the local jail on $1,563 bond.
      
    
            The Sun reports Jeffrey had a warrant out and was also arrested … and he's apparently being held on a $47,350 bond for 13 counts of misdemeanor forgery.
      
    
            Anna left "7 Little Johnstons" after season 16 because of her rocky relationship with her family.

title: Kelly Clarkson Store Feud: Art of Play Singing Bird Now on Sale for $15M
description:
Art of Play Owner
                          I'll Sell You My Bird ... for $15 Mil!!!
body:
Art of Play Owner
                          I'll Sell You My Bird ... for $15 Mil!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 14, 2026
                            3:09 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            After allegedly insisting to Kelly Clarkson that Molly the singing bird wasn't for sale, Art of Play is singing a different tune ... the art installation is now on sale ... with a $15 million price tag.
      
    
            This is the very bird at the center of Kelly's feud with shop co-owner Adam Rubin ... the piece sparked a big ol' he-said, she-said about whether or not Molly was ever actually for sale ... and now the Brooklyn shop is looking for a buyer with deep pockets.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Quick feud recap ... Adam insisted Molly was permanently attached to the wall and therefore not for sale. He claimed the artist who designed the bird would be willing to sell "Molly's twin" for $15K and said he offered Kelly a different bird automaton for $2,000 that she could bring home that day, but she left without taking a look.
      

            Kelly, however, claims Adam's full of crap ... she says the store owners treated her like Julia Roberts' character in "Pretty Woman."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Adam ripped Kelly on Tuesday, and on Wednesday our photog stopped by the Brooklyn toy shop and discovered Molly was on sale ... for $15M.
      
    
            The description reads, in part ... "The world's most famous singing bird automata!"
      
    
            No word if Kelly's still interested.
